hero.headline: Where care is far, and who can least afford the distance.
hero.subhead: Sehhatlas maps two things for every region of Saudi Arabia — how easily people can reach healthcare, and how vulnerable they are if they can't — and shows exactly where those two problems overlap.

dataStrip.caption: All Phase 1 inputs are publicly available. No permissions required.

values.heading: What sets this apart
values.subheading: Four decisions that shape how the platform is built.

cards.title: Access, not counts
cards.body: A facility count per region says nothing about how far anyone actually travels. The access score is a two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) measure — how many facilities a population can reach within 30 or 60 minutes, discounted by how many other people compete for the same facilities.

cards.title: A vulnerability index that doesn't exist yet
cards.body: No published small-area socioeconomic vulnerability index exists for Saudi Arabia. This one combines census socioeconomic data, satellite environmental exposure, and chronic disease burden into a single, standardised measure.

cards.title: Two axes, not one score
cards.body: Access and vulnerability are kept deliberately separate. Merging them into one number would hide which problem a planner is looking at — distance, need, or both — and those require different interventions.

cards.title: Open and reproducible by design
cards.body: Every input is freely available data. Every method is published. Anyone — a ministry planner, an academic reviewer, another researcher — can check the work or reproduce it end to end.

byNumbers.heading: By the numbers
byNumbers.subheading: What Phase 1 is built to work across, per the MOH Statistical Yearbook 2024 and the 2022 GASTAT census.

tiers.heading: The platform
tiers.subheading: Two tiers, deliberately kept separate — different audiences, different risk profiles.

cards.title: Planning tier
cards.body: Planner- and researcher-facing. Built entirely on static, open data. Complete in itself: facility validation, both axes, the quadrant classification, and internal validation.

cards.title: Siting optimiser
cards.body: Location-allocation modelling recommending where new clinics would relieve the most unmet need, using institutional data under a KAIMRC IRB.

cards.title: Patient tier
cards.body: A patient-facing map of nearby emergency departments and current occupancy. Requires live hospital feeds, SFDA clearance, and emergency physician oversight — none of which exist yet.

journey.subheading: The workflow a planner follows once both axes are computed.

steps.title: Measure
steps.body: Compute the access score and the vulnerability index independently for every region, validated against official facility statistics.

steps.title: Classify
steps.body: Plot both scores against each other. The quadrant a region falls into — not either score alone — tells a planner what kind of problem they're looking at.

steps.title: Act
steps.body: Prioritise the high-vulnerability, low-access quadrant first. In later phases, a siting optimiser recommends where a new facility would help most.

closingCta.heading: Working on health access in Saudi Arabia? Let's talk.

hero.title: A planning tool for a question no one was answering.
hero.subtitle: Sehhatlas is developed independently by a student researcher, applying open geospatial data to a gap in how Saudi Arabia measures healthcare access.

mission.heading: Mission
mission.body: To give health planners, researchers, and policymakers in Saudi Arabia a free, open, and reproducible way to see where healthcare access and population vulnerability overlap — so that scarce siting and outreach resources go to the communities that need them most, not just the ones a raw facility count makes visible.

problem.heading: The problem
paragraphs: Saudi Arabia publishes how many hospitals and health centres exist in each of its 13 administrative regions — 516 hospitals and 5,779 primary healthcare centres per the MOH Statistical Yearbook 2024, against a 2022 census population of 32,175,224. But a facility count divided by an administrative boundary answers none of the questions a planner faces.

It does not say how far anyone actually travels to reach care, whether the nearest facility is already saturated by everyone else competing for it, or whether the populations facing the longest journeys are the ones least able to make them. A wealthy household drives ninety minutes to a hospital without difficulty; a poor household experiences the same ninety minutes as a barrier that delays treatment until it becomes an emergency.

On every existing measure, those two places look identical. No published tool currently distinguishes them anywhere in the Kingdom, and no small-area socioeconomic vulnerability index exists for Saudi Arabia at all.

founder.heading: Founder
founder.name: Hamad Al-Zuhayri

founder.bio: Hamad is a sixth-year medical student at King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences in Riyadh, with research access through the Ministry of National Guard Health Affairs. Sehhatlas began with a question raised during clinical training: the Kingdom publishes how many facilities each region has, but nothing about who can actually reach them. Phase 1 is deliberately built on open data, so that every step of the method can be checked and reproduced by anyone.

institutional.heading: Institutional context
institutional.body: Sehhatlas is developed independently by a student researcher at King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences (KSAU-HS), with research access through the Ministry of National Guard Health Affairs (MNGHA) for later phases. KSAU-HS and MNGHA are named here as affiliations and, in later phases, potential data-access routes — not as endorsers, funders, owners, or partners of this platform.

hero.title: Two independent measures. One priority map.
hero.subtitle: How the access score and the vulnerability index are built, why they're kept apart, and what still needs work.

access.title: Axis 1 — Spatial access to healthcare
access.body: A two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) score: not facility counts, but how many facilities a population can reach within 30 or 60 minutes of travel, discounted by how many other people compete for the same facilities.
inputs: OpenStreetMap facility locations and road network
MOH facility statistics, used for validation

vulnerability.title: Axis 2 — Vulnerability
vulnerability.body: A constructed index combining three components, standardised and combined by principal component analysis (PCA) with published loadings. The reasoning: these compound one another. A community that is poor, heat-exposed, and already managing chronic illness carries far more health need than one that is merely distant, because chronic conditions demand sustained nearby care and distance turns that management into emergency presentation.

components.title: Socioeconomic
components.body: Census data on education, housing, and income.

components.title: Environmental exposure
components.body: Satellite data on PM2.5 air pollution, heat, and greenery (NDVI, Normalized Difference Vegetation Index).

components.title: Chronic disease burden
components.body: Principally diabetes and hypertension, from national health surveys.

quadrant.heading: The quadrant
quadrant.body: Every unit is plotted on both axes, splitting the map into four groups. The two numbers are deliberately kept separate rather than merged into one score, because the quadrant tells a planner not just where the problem is but which problem they are looking at — and those need different interventions.

priority.title: Priority
priority.subtitle: High vulnerability, low access
priority.body: Far from care and least equipped to cope with being far. The target group for siting and outreach.

served.title: Served but vulnerable
served.subtitle: High vulnerability, good access
served.body: Access isn't the barrier here — the underlying vulnerability is. Needs outreach and chronic-care support, not new facilities.

remote.title: Remote but resourced
remote.subtitle: Low vulnerability, low access
remote.body: Distant, but the population can generally absorb it. Lower priority than the priority quadrant.

none.title: No identified gap
none.subtitle: Low vulnerability, good access
none.body: Neither access nor vulnerability stands out. Not a priority for new intervention.

whyTwoAxes.heading: Why two axes, not one score
whyTwoAxes.body: A single blended score would be easier to rank — and would hide the thing a planner most needs to know. Two regions can produce the same combined score for entirely different reasons: one because it's remote but resilient, the other because it's nearby but overwhelmed by need. Collapsing that distinction into one number erases the difference between 'build a clinic here' and 'fund outreach and chronic-disease management here.' Keeping the axes separate keeps that distinction visible.

validation.heading: Validation approach
validation.body: Because chronic disease sits inside the vulnerability score, it cannot also be used to test that score. Validation instead relies on three approaches, in order of what's currently feasible:

items.title: Facility validation
items.body: The OpenStreetMap facility layer is checked against official MOH figures, region by region, producing a coverage ratio that shows where the map is reliable.

items.title: Leave-one-component-out sensitivity analysis
items.body: The vulnerability index is recomputed with each component removed in turn, to see how much any single input drives the result.

items.title: Expert face-validity review
items.body: Regional public health practitioners review whether the classification matches what they observe on the ground.

items.title: Clinical outcome validation (later phase)
items.body: Testing the index against measured outcomes such as emergency department utilisation and avoidable admissions, once institutional data access is in place.

tier1.title: Tier 1 — Planning tier
tier1.body: Planner- and researcher-facing. Built entirely on static, open data. Buildable now, and complete in itself. This is Phase 1.

tier2.title: Tier 2 — Patient tier
tier2.body: Patient-facing: a map showing nearby emergency departments and how busy each currently is, plus a short triage questionnaire feeding an estimated wait time — so a patient isn't forced to default to the closest ED when a quieter one is reachable.
safety: Anyone reporting chest pain, stroke symptoms, or other red-flag presentations is instructed to call 997 and attend the nearest facility, with all routing suppressed.
Wait times, when shown, are always ranges — never precise figures.

This tier requires live occupancy feeds from hospitals, SFDA clearance as clinical decision support, and emergency physician oversight — none of which currently exist. The realistic entry point is a single-cluster pilot, not a national launch.
This tier is not available. Nothing on this site should be used to decide where to seek care.

rows.provides: Night-time lights, as an economic activity proxy
Reanalysis climate data, including heat exposure

limitations.heading: Limitations
items: OpenStreetMap facility coverage is uneven and weakest in rural areas; the validation module quantifies this rather than hiding it.
Chronic disease data exists only at 13-region resolution with wide confidence intervals; governorate-level small-area estimation is the priority methodological upgrade.
Thirteen regions is too few units for stable spatial modelling; governorate-level analysis (roughly 139 units) is strongly preferred, contingent on obtaining boundary polygons.
Phase 1 has no external validation against clinical outcomes; this is stated, not hidden, and is planned for a later phase.
Income is not a census variable in Saudi Arabia and may need to be proxied by other socioeconomic indicators.

hero.title: Methodology notes
hero.subtitle: Written for an academic reader. Full detail will accompany the Phase 1 manuscript.

sections.title: 2SFCA (two-step floating catchment area)
sections.body: The access score is computed in two steps. First, for each facility, a facility-to-population ratio is calculated using all population within the facility's catchment (a 30 or 60-minute travel-time threshold). Second, for each population point, the access score sums the facility-to-population ratios of every facility within reach of that point. This produces a per-capita measure of available capacity, not a raw distance or a facility count.

sections.title: PCA-based index construction
sections.body: The vulnerability index standardises each input component (socioeconomic, environmental, disease burden) to a common scale, then combines them using principal component analysis (PCA). The first principal component's loadings — published alongside the index — determine each component's contribution to the final score.

sections.title: Tercile cut-points
sections.body: Regions are classified into 'high' and 'low' groups on each axis using tercile cuts by default, with a median-cut toggle available for comparison. Cut-point choice affects which regions fall into the priority quadrant, particularly near the boundary — this is disclosed, not smoothed over.

sections.title: Multi-scale sensitivity
sections.body: Where boundary data permits, results are checked across administrative scales (region versus governorate) to see whether the classification is an artefact of the chosen unit size.

sections.title: MAUP and the ecological fallacy
sections.body: The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) means that results can shift depending on how boundaries are drawn — a caveat that applies to any areal analysis, including this one. Region-level classification also carries an ecological fallacy risk: a conclusion true of a region as a whole is not necessarily true of every community, or every person, within it. Both are stated explicitly rather than implied away by a confident-looking map.
